questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: In the circuit of figure, the power dissipated in the resistor R is 1W when only source '1' is present and '2' is replaced by a short. The power dissipated in the same resistor R is 4W when only source '2' is present and '1' is replaced by a short. When both the sources '1' and '2' are present, the power dissipated in R will be :
questions.explanation:
Case 1: Only Source 1 is active (Source 2 is short-circuited)
The power dissipated in resistor \(R\) is given as \(P_{1} = 1\,\text{W}\). \[P_{1} = |I_{1}|^2 \times R\] \[1 = |I_{1}|^2 \times 1 \implies |I_{1}| = 1\,\text{A}\] Looking at the polarity of Source 1, the reference direction for the current phasor \(I_{1}\) flowing downward through \(R\) can be written as: \[I_{1} = -|I_{1}| = -1\,\text{A}\] Case 2: Only Source 2 is active (Source 1 is short-circuited)
The power dissipated in resistor \(R\) is given as \(P_{2} = 4\,\text{W}\). \[P_{2} = |I_{2}|^2 \times R\] \[4 = |I_{2}|^2 \times 1 \implies |I_{2}| = 2\,\text{A}\] Looking at the polarity of Source 2, the reference direction for the current phasor \(I_{2}\) flowing downward through \(R\) can be written as: \[I_{2} = +|I_{2}| = 2\,\text{A}\] Case 3: Both sources are active simultaneously
Since both sources operate at the same frequency \(\omega\), we can algebraically combine the parallel current contributions using superposition: \[I_{\text{total}} = I_{1} + I_{2}\] \[I_{\text{total}} = -1 + 2 = 1\,\text{A}\] The total power \(P_{\text{total}}\) dissipated in resistor \(R\) is: \[P_{\text{total}} = |I_{\text{total}}|^2 \times R\] \[P_{\text{total}} = (1)^2 \times 1 = 1\,\text{W}\] \[\boxed{(a) 1 W}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: A load \(Z_L = R_L+jX_L\) is to be matched, using an ideal transformer to a generator of internal impedance, \(Z_S = R_S+jX_S\). The turns ratio of the transformer required is
questions.explanation:
To match a complex load impedance \(Z_{l} = R_{l} + jX_{l}\) to a source with an internal impedance \(Z_{s} = R_{s} + jX_{s}\) using an ideal transformer, we look at how the transformer transforms magnitudes. An ideal transformer with a primary-to-secondary turns ratio of \(n = \frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}\) alters the secondary load impedance when viewed from its primary side. The reflected load impedance \(Z_{l}'\) connected across the primary terminals is given by: \[Z_{l}' = n^2 Z_{l}\] Taking the absolute magnitude of both sides: \[|Z_{l}'| = n^2 |Z_{l}|\] For maximum power transfer matching between a source and its reflected load network when transforming through an ideal transformer, the magnitude of the reflected load impedance must equal the magnitude of the internal source impedance (\(|Z_{l}'| = |Z_{s}|\)): \[|Z_{s}| = n^2 |Z_{l}|\] Solving for the turns ratio \(n^2\): \[n^2 = \frac{|Z_{s}|}{|Z_{l}|}\] Inverting the relationship depending on the reference conversion direction matching primary-to-secondary configurations: \[n = \sqrt{\left|\frac{Z_{l}}{Z_{s}}\right|}\] \[\boxed{(a)\sqrt{|Z_L/Z_S|}}\]
Key points
  • An ideal transformer acts as an impedance matching device changing the impedance scale by the square of its turns ratio (\(n^2\)).
  • It can change only the magnitude of a complex load, not its phase angle, because it lacks reactive components.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse simple transformer impedance transformation with conjugate impedance matching (\(Z_{l} = Z_{s}^*\)). An ideal transformer alone cannot cancel out the reactive component unless the transformation matches the overall absolute magnitudes.

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: The half-power bandwidth of the resonant circuit of figure can be increased by
questions.explanation: To determine how to increase the half-power bandwidth of the given resonant circuit, we evaluate the circuit's parallel resonance characteristics and its quality factor relationships. The half-power bandwidth (\(\text{BW}\)) of a resonant circuit is fundamentally related to its resonant frequency (\(\omega_{0}\)) and its quality factor (\(Q_{0}\)): \[\text{BW} = \frac{\omega_{0}}{Q_{0}}\] For an ideal parallel resonant tank circuit containing a capacitance \(C\) in parallel with an equivalent resistance \(R_{\text{eq}}\), the quality factor is expressed as: \[Q_{0} = \omega_{0} R_{\text{eq}} C\] Substituting \(Q_{0}\) back into the bandwidth equation shows that bandwidth depends inversely on the total parallel equivalent resistance: \[\text{BW} = \frac{\omega_{0}}{\omega_{0} R_{\text{eq}} C} = \frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}} C}\] Thus, to increase the half-power bandwidth (\(\text{BW}\)), the total equivalent parallel resistance \(R_{\text{eq}}\) must be decreased. NOTE : \(R_{eq}\) is the effective resistance as seen by the capacitance C. Let us analyze how changing \(R_{1}\) and \(R_{2}\) impacts the equivalent parallel damping: 1. Effect of \(R_{2}\): Resistor \(R_{2}\) is connected directly in parallel with the capacitive branch. A direct decrease in the value of \(R_{2}\) will lower the overall parallel combination resistance \(R_{\text{eq}}\). \[R_{\text{eq}} \approx R_{\text{series-converted}} \parallel R_{2}\] Decreasing \(R_{2}\) directly causes \(R_{\text{eq}}\) to decrease, which consequently increases the bandwidth. Thus, Option D is correct. 2. Effect of \(R_{1}\): The inductive branch contains a series resistance \(R_{1}\). To find its parallel equivalence near resonance, we perform a series-to-parallel transformation of the practical inductor branch (\(R_{1}\) in series with \(L\)). The equivalent parallel resistance \(R_{p1}\) contributed by this branch is: \[R_{p1} = R_{1} \left(1 + Q_{\text{coil}}^2\right) = R_{1} \left(1 + \frac{\omega^2 L^2}{R_{1}^2}\right) = R_{1} + \frac{\omega^2 L^2}{R_{1}}\] Near resonance, assuming a reasonably high coil quality factor (\(Q_{\text{coil}} \gg 1\)): \[R_{p1} \approx \frac{\omega_{0}^2 L^2}{R_{1}}\] The overall equivalent parallel resistance \(R_{\text{eq}}\) of the entire network becomes: \[R_{\text{eq}} = R_{p1} \parallel R_{2} = \left(\frac{\omega_{0}^2 L^2}{R_{1}}\right) \parallel R_{2}\] From this expression, if we increase \(R_{1}\), the value of the equivalent parallel resistance \(R_{p1}\) drops. A decrease in \(R_{p1}\) lowers the total parallel combination resistance \(R_{\text{eq}}\). Since a lower \(R_{\text{eq}}\) increases the bandwidth: \[\text{BW} \uparrow \ \implies R_{\text{eq}} \downarrow \ \implies R_{p1} \downarrow \ \implies R_{1} \uparrow\] Therefore, increasing \(R_{1}\) also serves to increase the bandwidth. Thus, Option A is correct. \[\boxed{(a)increasing \,R_1\,, (b)decreasing \,R_2}\]

questions.question: The concentration of ionized acceptors and donors in a semiconductor are \(N_A\), \(N_D\) respectively. If \(N_A > N_D\) and \(n_i\) is the intrinsic concentration, the position of the Fermi level with respect to the intrinsic level depends on
questions.explanation: The Fermi level position is given by \[E_i - E_F = kT \ln \left( \frac{N_A - N_D}{n_i} \right)\], which directly depends on the net doping concentration \(N_A - N_D\). Since \(N_A > N_D\), the semiconductor is p-type and the Fermi level shifts toward the valence band based on this difference. \[\boxed{(A) \, N_A - N_D}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: Due to illumination by light, the electron and hole concentrations in a heavily doped \(N\) type semiconductor increases by \(\Delta n\) and \(\Delta p\) respectively if \(n_i\) is the intrinsic concentration then,
questions.explanation:
When a semiconductor is illuminated by light with photon energy greater than the bandgap energy (\(E_{ph} > E_{g}\)), valence electrons absorb the energy and move to the conduction band. This process generates electron-hole pairs (EHPs). Due to the nature of this generation process, for every electron that is excited to the conduction band, a corresponding hole is created in the valence band. Therefore, the increase in carrier concentrations must be equal: \[\Delta n = \Delta p\] where,
  • \(\Delta n = \text{increase in electron concentration due to illumination}\)
  • \(\Delta p = \text{increase in hole concentration due to illumination}\)
\[\boxed{(C) \, \Delta n = \Delta p}\]

options: the mobility of minority carriers in the \(P^+\) region.
the lifetime of minority carriers in the \(P^+\) region.
the mobility of majority carriers in the \(N\) region.
the lifetime of majority carriers in the \(N\) region.
questions.note: Marks awarded to all (official key: MTA)
questions.explanation: In a \(P^+N\) junction, the heavily doped \(P^+\) side injects very few electrons into itself, while most excess charge storage occurs due to holes injected into the lightly doped \(N\) region. Hence, switching speed mainly depends on the minority carrier lifetime in the N region, which is not among the given options. \[\boxed{MTA}\]

questions.question: Refer to figure shown below
questions.explanation:
Given circuit consist of two diodes and initially at \(t = 0\) the states of diode are unknown so it is indetermine system. Case 1 : When \(V_i > 0\), then
\[\left[ \begin{array}{c} \text{Inverting terminal} \\ \text{voltage } (V_-) \end{array} \right] > \left[ \begin{array}{c} \text{Non-inverting} \\ \text{terminal voltage } (V_+) \end{array} \right]\] Then, \(V_0'\) goes towards negative saturation. When \(V_0' = -0.7\,\text{V}\), then diode \(D_1\) becomes forward biased i.e. ON (forward voltage drop = \(0.7\,\text{V}\)). Diode \(D_2\) becomes reverse biased i.e. OFF (Open circuit). Hence, the modified circuit is shown below, Virtual ground concept is valid for Negative feedback closed system. From virtual ground concept, \[V_- = V_+ = 0\] Since, entire current \(I_1\) is flowing through the diode \(D_1\). So, \(I_2 = 0\,\text{A}\) From figure, \(I_2 = \frac{0 - V_0}{R_2} = 0\). Hence, \(V_0 = -0 \times R_2 = 0\,\text{V}\) Case 2 : When \(V_i < 0\), then
\[\left[ \begin{array}{c} \text{Inverting terminal} \\ \text{voltage } (V_-) \end{array} \right] < \left[ \begin{array}{c} \text{Non-inverting} \\ \text{terminal voltage } (V_+) \end{array} \right]\] Then, \(V_0'\) goes towards positive saturation. When \(V_0' = 0.7\,\text{V}\), then diode \(D_1\) becomes reverse biased i.e. OFF (Open circuit). Diode \(D_2\) becomes forward biased i.e. ON (forward voltage drop = \(0.7\,\text{V}\)). Hence, the modified circuit is shown below, From the virtual ground concept, \[V_- = V_A = V_+ = 0\] Modified circuit represents inverting Op-Amp circuit. Hence, output of inverting Op-Amp circuit is given by, \[V_0 = \frac{-R_2}{R_1} \times V_i\] From case 1 and case 2, output voltage \(V_0\) can be written as given below, \[V_0 = \begin{cases} 0 & ; \quad V_i \geq 0\,\text{V} \\ \frac{-R_2}{R_1}V_i & ; \quad V_i \leq 0\,\text{V} \end{cases}\] \[\boxed{ \begin{aligned} \text{(B)}\;& \text{For } V_i>0,\quad V_0=0 \\ \text{(C)}\;& \text{For } V_i<0,\quad V_0=-\frac{R_2}{R_1}V_i \end{aligned} }\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Families and Semiconductor Memories Q1
questions.question: A logic family has threshold voltage \(V_T = 2\text{ V}\), minimum guaranteed output high voltage \(V_{OH} = 4\text{ V}\), minimum accepted input high voltage \(V_{IH} = 3\text{ V}\), maximum guaranteed output low voltage \(V_{OL} = 1\text{ V}\), and maximum accepted input low voltage \(V_{IL} = 1.5\text{ V}\). Its noise margin is
questions.explanation:
To determine the total noise margin (\(NM\)) of a logic family, we need to calculate both the high-level noise margin (\((NM)_H\)) and the low-level noise margin (\((NM)_L\)), and then select the minimum of the two values. Given parameters from the problem statement:
  • Threshold voltage, \(V_T = 2\,\text{V}\)
  • Minimum guaranteed output high voltage, \(V_{OH} = 4\,\text{V}\)
  • Minimum accepted input high voltage, \(V_{IH} = 3\,\text{V}\)
  • Maximum guaranteed output low voltage, \(V_{OL} = 1\,\text{V}\)
  • Maximum accepted input low voltage, \(V_{IL} = 1.5\,\text{V}\)
The formulations for the noise margins are defined as:
  1. High-Level Noise Margin (\((NM)_H\)):
    \[(NM)_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH}\] \[(NM)_H = 4\,\text{V} - 3\,\text{V} = 1\,\text{V}\]
  2. Low-Level Noise Margin (\((NM)_L\)):
    \[(NM)_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL}\] \[(NM)_L = 1.5\,\text{V} - 1\,\text{V} = 0.5\,\text{V}\]
The overall noise margin is the worst-case configuration, which corresponds to the minimum value: \[NM = \min\left[(NM)_H, (NM)_L\right]\] \[NM = \min(1\,\text{V}, 0.5\,\text{V}) = 0.5\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{\text{(D) 0.5 V}}\]
Key points
  • Physical Definition: Noise margin acts as a quantitative measure of the noise immunity of a digital circuit. It represents the maximum spurious noise voltage amplitude that can be added to an input signal without corrupting the intended logic level.
  • Design Rule Constraints: For stable, noise-tolerant hardware operation, the voltage bounds must strictly adhere to \(V_{OH} > V_{IH} > V_{IL} > V_{OL}\).

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: In a microprocessor system, the stack is used for
options: storing the program return address whenever a sub-routine jump instruction is executed.
storing all important CPU register contents whenever an interrupt is to be serviced.
storing program instructions for interrupt service routines.
questions.explanation:
The stack is a reserved portion of the main memory (RAM) used for temporary storage of binary data during program execution.
  • When a subroutine jump instruction (such as CALL) is executed, the microprocessor automatically pushes the contents of the Program Counter (PC)---which represents the program return address---onto the stack.
  • Upon executing a return instruction (such as RET), this return address is popped back into the PC to resume normal program flow.
\[\boxed{\text{(A) storing the program return address whenever a subroutine jump instruction is executed.}}\]
Key points
  • Subroutine Call: Saves the return address (PC contents) onto the stack automatically.
  • Register Storage: Although registers can be saved using PUSH instructions, the CPU does not automatically save all important register contents during an interrupt unless explicitly programmed.

questions.question: In order to stabilize the system shown in fig. \(T_i\) should satisfy:

From the given block diagram, the forward path transfer function \(G(s)\) is: \[G(s) = \left(\frac{1 + sT_i}{s}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{1}{s(1 + sT)}\right) = \frac{1 + sT_i}{s^2(1 + sT)}\] The characteristic equation of this unity feedback system (\(H(s) = 1\)) is defined by \(1 + G(s)H(s) = 0\): \[1 + \frac{1 + sT_i}{s^2(1 + sT)} = 0 \implies s^3T + s^2 + sT_i + 1 = 0\] RH Table : \[\begin{array}{c|cc}
  s^3 & T & T_i \\
  s^2 & 1 & 1 \\
  s^1 & T_i - T & 0 \\
  s^0 & 1 & 0
\end{array}\] For absolute closed-loop stability, all elements in the first column of the Routh array must be strictly positive. Assuming the physical time constant \(T > 0\), From \(s^1\) row: \[T_i - T > 0 \implies T_i > T\] \[\boxed{(D)\ \ T_i > T}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: Zero mean Gaussian noise of variance \(N\) is applied to a half wave rectifier. The mean squared value of the rectifier output will be:
questions.explanation: Theory: In half-wave rectification, all negative values are clipped to zero while positive values remain unchanged. Hence the output PDF contains a delta function at the origin along with the positive half of the Gaussian PDF. Half wave rectification is represented as \[Y=X \qquad \text{for } x\geq 0\] \[Y=0 \qquad \text{for } x<0\]Therefore, the probability density function of \(Y\) is \[f(y)=\frac{1}{2}\delta(y)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi N}}e^{-y^2/2N}\]The mean square value is \[E(Y^2)=\int_{0}^{\infty} y^2 f(y)\,dy\] \[=\int_{0}^{\infty} y^2 \left[ \frac{1}{2}\delta(y)+ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi N}}e^{-y^2/2N} \right]dy\]Since, \[y^2\delta(y)=0\]we get \[E(Y^2)= \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{y^2}{\sqrt{2\pi N}} e^{-y^2/2N}\,dy\]Let \[\frac{y}{\sqrt{N}}=t\]Then, \[y=\sqrt{N}\,t, \qquad dy=\sqrt{N}\,dt\]Substituting, \[E(Y^2)= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi N}} \int_{0}^{\infty} Nt^2 e^{-t^2/2}\sqrt{N}\,dt\] \[= \frac{N}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty} t^2 e^{-t^2/2}\,dt\]Using the standard Gaussian integral, \[\int_{0}^{\infty} t^2 e^{-t^2/2}\,dt = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\]Therefore, \[E(Y^2)= \frac{N}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}} = \frac{N}{2}\] \[\boxed{(B) E(Y^2)=\frac{N}{2} }\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A source produces 4 symbols with probabilities \[\frac{1}{2},\quad \frac{1}{4},\quad \frac{1}{8},\quad \frac{1}{8}.\]For this source, a practical coding scheme has an average codeword length of \[L=2 \text{ bits/symbol}.\]The efficiency of the code is
questions.explanation: Theory: The efficiency of a source code is defined as \[\eta=\frac{H}{L},\]where \[H=\text{source entropy}, \qquad L=\text{average codeword length}.\] Calculating the source entropy, \[H = -\sum_i p_i\log_2 p_i.\]Substituting the given probabilities, \[H = -\left[ \frac12\log_2\frac12 + \frac14\log_2\frac14 + \frac18\log_2\frac18 + \frac18\log_2\frac18 \right].\]Using \[\log_2\frac12=-1, \qquad \log_2\frac14=-2, \qquad \log_2\frac18=-3,\]we obtain \[H = \frac12(1) + \frac14(2) + \frac18(3) + \frac18(3).\] \[H = \frac12+\frac12+\frac38+\frac38.\] \[H = \frac74 =1.75 \text{ bits/symbol}.\]Given \[L=2 \text{ bits/symbol},\]therefore \[\eta = \frac{H}{L} = \frac{1.75}{2} = 0.875.\]Hence, \[\boxed{(B) \eta=\frac78}.\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A signal \(x(t)=2\cos(\pi\cdot10^4t)\) volts is applied to an FM modulator with the sensitivity constant of \(10\ \text{kHz/volt}\). Then the modulation index of the FM wave is
questions.explanation:
Theory: The FM modulation index equals the ratio of frequency deviation to the modulating frequency. Given,\[k_f=10~\text{kHz/volt},\]\[A_m=2~\text{V}.\]From\[x(t)=2\cos(\pi\times10^4t),\]\[\omega_m=\pi\times10^4,\]therefore,\[f_m=\frac{\omega_m}{2\pi}=5~\text{kHz}.\]The frequency deviation is\[\Delta f=k_fA_m =10\times2 =20~\text{kHz}.\]Hence,\[\beta=\frac{\Delta f}{f_m} = \frac{20}{5} = 4.\]Therefore,\[\boxed{(A) \beta=4}\]
Key points
  • Frequency deviation is \(\Delta f=k_fA_m\).
  • FM modulation index is \(\beta=\dfrac{\Delta f}{f_m}\).
  • Convert angular frequency to frequency before applying the formula.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use \(\omega_m\) directly in place of \(f_m\).
  • Do not forget to multiply sensitivity by message amplitude to obtain \(\Delta f\).
  • Remember that \(f_m=\dfrac{\omega_m}{2\pi}\).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The skin depth of copper at a frequency of \(3\text{ GHz}\) is \(1\text{ micro } (10^{-6}\text{ meter})\). At \(12\text{ GHz}\), for a non magnetic conductor whose conductivity is \(1/9\) times that of copper, the skin depth would be
questions.explanation:
The skin depth \(\delta\) of a good conductor is defined by the formula: \[\delta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f \mu \sigma}}\] From this relation, it is evident that skin depth is inversely proportional to the square root of the product of frequency \(f\) and conductivity \(\sigma\): \[\delta \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{f\sigma}}\] Using the ratio of two states, we can relate the changes in frequency and conductivity to the change in skin depth: \[\frac{\delta_{2}}{\delta_{1}} = \sqrt{\frac{f_{1}\sigma_{1}}{f_{2}\sigma_{2}}}\] Given parameters:
  • \(\delta_{1} = 1\,\mu\text{m}\)
  • \(f_{1} = 3\,\text{GHz}\), \(f_{2} = 12\,\text{GHz}\)
  • \(\frac{\sigma_{2}}{\sigma_{1}} = \frac{1}{9} \implies \frac{\sigma_{1}}{\sigma_{2}} = 9\)
Substituting these into the ratio equation: \[\frac{\delta_{2}}{1\,\mu\text{m}} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{3}{12}\right) \times 9} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4} \times 9} = \sqrt{\frac{9}{4}}\] \[\delta_{2} = \frac{3}{2}\,\mu\text{m} = 1.5\,\mu\text{m}\] \[\boxed{(B):1.5\,\mu\text{m}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A \(50\ \Omega\) lossless transmission line has a pure reactance of \((j100)\ \Omega\) as its load. The VSWR in the line is
questions.explanation: The reflection coefficient (\(\Gamma\)) and the Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR) for a transmission line terminated with a load impedance \(Z_{L} = j100\,\Omega\) and characteristic impedance \(Z_{0} = 50\,\Omega\) are calculated as follows: \[\Gamma = \frac{Z_{L} - Z_{0}}{Z_{L} + Z_{0}} = \frac{j100 - 50}{j100 + 50}\] Taking the magnitude of the complex reflection coefficient: \[|\Gamma| = \frac{\sqrt{(100)^2 + (-50)^2}}{\sqrt{(100)^2 + (50)^2}} = \frac{\sqrt{10000 + 2500}}{\sqrt{10000 + 2500}} = 1\] Now, calculating the VSWR: \[\text{VSWR} = \frac{1 + |\Gamma|}{1 - |\Gamma|} = \frac{1 + 1}{1 - 1} = \frac{2}{0} = \infty\] \[\boxed{(D):\infty}\]
